questions.q: Define global sequence alignment and state one biological scenario where it is the appropriate choice.
questions.a: Global alignment aligns two sequences from end to end, maximizing matches across their entire lengths. It is appropriate when comparing full-length orthologous genes or proteins of similar length (e.g., comparing the complete cytochrome c sequences of human and yeast). A wrong answer (e.g., "global alignment finds the best local match") reveals confusion with local alignment and indicates the student cannot distinguish the fundamental scope difference.

questions.q: Explain why a researcher studying a conserved protein domain across diverse species would choose local alignment over global alignment.
questions.a: Local alignment identifies the highest-scoring matching subsequences without requiring the rest of the sequences to align. If only a single domain (e.g., a kinase domain) is conserved while flanking regions differ in length and composition, global alignment would force alignment of non-homologous regions, introducing excessive gaps and lowering the overall score. A wrong answer (e.g., "local alignment is faster") shows the student focuses on computational convenience rather than biological appropriateness.

questions.q: Two protein sequences share 40% identity over their full lengths but have a 90% identical region of 50 amino acids in the middle. Which alignment type would yield a higher similarity score for that 50-aa region, and why?
questions.a: Local alignment would yield a higher score for the 50-aa region because it evaluates only the best-matching segment, ignoring the poorly matching flanking regions. Global alignment averages the score across the entire length, diluting the high local similarity. A wrong answer (e.g., "global alignment gives a higher score because it covers more sequence") indicates misunderstanding of how scoring works across alignment types.

questions.q: Compare the effect of increasing the gap opening penalty in global vs. local alignment. How does it differently impact the resulting alignments?
questions.a: In global alignment, a high gap opening penalty forces fewer, longer gaps to maintain end-to-end alignment, potentially forcing mismatches in non-homologous regions. In local alignment, a high gap opening penalty may prevent the extension of a high-scoring segment into adjacent lower-similarity regions, causing the algorithm to report multiple separate high-scoring pairs instead of one longer alignment. A wrong answer (e.g., "it has the same effect in both") shows the student does not grasp how the alignment objective (global vs. local) interacts with gap penalties.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since local alignment finds the best match, it is always better than global alignment." Evaluate this statement with a counterexample.
questions.a: The statement is false. When comparing two full-length orthologs of similar length (e.g., human and mouse beta-globin), global alignment correctly captures the overall evolutionary divergence across the entire sequence. Local alignment might only report the most conserved exon, missing differences in other regions that are biologically meaningful. A wrong evaluation (e.g., agreeing with the student) reveals an inability to match method to biological context.

questions.q: Design a mini-project: You have sequenced a novel viral genome and want to identify all known protein domains in it. Outline the alignment strategy (global/local), database, and tool you would use, and justify each choice.
questions.a: Use local alignment (e.g., BLASTP) against a protein domain database (e.g., Pfam or CDD) because viral genomes are compact and may contain multiple domains in different reading frames; global alignment would fail due to length mismatches and non-homologous regions. A poor answer (e.g., "use global alignment against GenBank") shows the student cannot translate a real-world problem into appropriate bioinformatics choices.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Sequence alignment is the ______ arrangement of two or more biological sequences (DNA, RNA, or protein) to identify regions of similarity that may indicate functional, structural, or evolutionary relationships.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have two DNA ______ from different bacteria: one is 1,200 bp long, the other is 1,500 bp.
What is Sequence alignment? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Sequence alignment is the computational arrangement of two or more biological sequences (DNA, RNA, or protein) to identify regions of similarity that may indicate functional, structural, or evolutionary relationships.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Sequence alignment?
questions.a: Students often think "global alignment is for similar sequences, local for dissimilar ones." This is incorrect: global alignment is for comparing *entire* sequences (regardless of similarity), while local alignment is for finding *any* conserved region (even in highly similar sequences).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to distinguish between global and local alignment scenarios, justify the choice of alignment type for a given biological question (e.g., comparing full-length orthologs vs. finding conserved domains), and explain how gap penalties and scoring matrices influence the alignment outcome.
